[b]Full Disclosure[/b] I have so many hours in this game because I have been speedrunning it for 6 years. I've made several videos about this game as well. If you have ANY questions about the game at all, even technical, reach out to me and I will have an answer. This game is basically my adopted child at this point, so [b]this review IS BIASED.[/b]

[h1]What a Terrible Game[/h1]
Enclave is still totally beautiful. This hack and slash Action RPG was ahead of its time when it originally released in 2002. Starbreeze had a great engine, and a great team working on it. The level design is fantastic and non-linear, so there's a lot of depth to the levels, and you'll get lost exploring the engaging scenery and all the twists and turns of wherever the world can take you. There's 2 campaigns with a combined 31 levels total to go through (including bonus levels). The music is phenomenal and smoothly transitions based on if you are in combat or not. The game uses a money progression system in lieu of RPG levels so you can afford better equipment on future levels to deal more damage and take less. Finding the money is a hunt and one of the main challenges. If you find all 13,000 gold, you unlock a chick with a Rocket Launcher. 

A main complaint is about combat, but actually hit detection is true to the mesh of the characters and objects, which can unfortunately mean there's lots of missing. Aside from this, the 12 different classes you get to play as all have their own playstyles, especially with the Druid/Lich (Caster / Summoner), Huntress/Assassin (Archer / Sniper), and Engineer/Bombardier (Bombs and Bombs). Some classes also have advantages through their speed (Halfling / Goblin) and unique weapons available to them (Godly Poison bolts).

The story is kind of boilerplate fantasy. Here it is:
The lands are magical, and the demon lord Vatar wants to suck up the magic. There was a war 1000 years ago because of this. The wizard "Zale" put a halt to everything by causing a circular rift in the world which created the Enclave of Celenheim. The people of Celenheim got lazy and stupid over those 1000 years and forgot that the outlanders wanted their magic lands. Now the lands are healing themselves, and Vatar is like "Oh hey now we can cross again" so now there's a big battle ensuing over the land. Celenheim needs help from their allies if they want to stand a chance, but the allies are so isolated and far away, also there's a big outlander fortress blocking their way back. That's what you take care of on the Light Side. On the Dark side, you help some goth chick named Mordessa summon back Vatar through making a virgin sacrifice of the Celenheim princess, then you siege the hell out of them.

[b]The Assassin is the best character because she wears a mask, and so should you.[/b]

[h1]How long will you be entertained by this $5 game[/h1]
About 3-4 hours if you're just wanting to play through something casually. Get it for a day, stream it, have some fun. You will have fun.

Also, everyone plays as the druid because of her butt.

[h1] Information / Review English [/h1]

Enclave is an action adventure game developed by Starbreeze.

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

In the world ruled by magic, the peoples of light and darkness were separated from one another by an infinitely deep rift that split the earth as a result of war thousands of years ago. The land of Celenheim is rich and thriving. It forms an enclave of sincerity and order, surrounded by the disfigured and barren wastelands of darkness, the war-torn plains of the so-called Outlands. Over the centuries, however, the deep rift began to close again, and skirmishes between the powers of light and darkness along the border areas soon became commonplace. Now it is only a matter of time before these disputes turn into a merciless war.

Celenheim is fighting for survival. A group of men and women are sent on a dangerous journey in hopes of saving the enclave from destruction. Their adventure takes them through hostile territory in search of the people of Meckelon, their ancient ancestors, from whom they were separated long ago. Perhaps they will find in them the help they so desperately need.

But Mordessa, the dark and mysterious leader of the Outlands, plans to bring the old demon Vatar, who was then responsible for the division of the world, back from the depths of the underworld in order to claim the magical lands of Celenheim. To do this, she sends her servants to acquire an artifact of forbidden knowledge that has hitherto been hidden from humanity: the Book of Souls. With the contents of the book, she would hold the key to the underworld and powers beyond the ability of mortals.

[h1] Pro [/h1]

+ solid graphics
+ several playable characters
+ 2 campaigns
+ over 20 missions
+ good mission design
+ challenging boss fights
+ lots of hidden places & treasures
+ a touch of Shadow of the Colossus
+ manageable menus
+ purchase of equipment and weapons
+ Trading cards

[h1] Contra [/h1]

- Game is too hard
- can only be saved at the end of the level
- Objects hardly destructible
- stuttering sound

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Enclave offers you a varied and wonderful fantasy slaughter festival, but with rough edges.

THE BAD PART:

Clumsy Combat 
The most important part in this game, but devs basically destroyed it.

The Game's hit scan is based on player's cam angle, meaning, if u encounter enemies like goblins, you'll often have to look at the floor to get the best hit scan possible, thats pretty awful, since you must adjust your cam angle based on enemy's size.

Buggy physic system

Game’s level design also contains numerous physical based events, such as a wall being blown up, or a enemy throwing something at you, sometimes they can make you get stuck, and since you can’t save in the middle of a level, if this happens, you are done, you need to restart the whole level. PAIN.

Other

if you switch between desktop and enclave, the brightness and gamma will be reset at a fixed rate and can't be changed unless you go to the graphics menu, turn on/off any option to get your brightness back.

THE GOOD PART:

Art style
Just like those classic RPGs, such as Gothic III and M&M Messiah, Enclave had a strong art foundation just like them. Devs using beautiful, detailed textures and baked lighting to fill up the game world, you can see so many amazing details in those simple models, just like those good RPGs from the good old days, they made various textures to represent scenes like Church, Castle, Town, and Underworld, your eyes just never get bored in enclave

AI

Enemies act differently depending on how close you are. If you're far away from them, they'll switch to bow. when reloading, they will try to move around to avoid your attack too. [b][i]Enclave[/i][/b] is a fantasy action-adventure game. The rift that separated the Enclave of Magic from the Outlands is slowly closing, and heroes emerge from both sides, either to defend or conquer the Enclave.

[b]Pros[/b]: The game offers two campaigns, first the light campaign where you defend the Enclave from the invaders, and then the dark campaign where you are a minion seeking the glory of conquest. As the story progresses, you find or unlock additional equipment and up to six characters (per campaign) to play as. At the start of each chapters, you get to pick your character and equipment, limited by how much gold you found in each mission. For the most part, you can backtrack as much as you want for each missions, and replay any of them at any time if you missed out on some gold and want to try to do better (allowing you to select more equipment).

[b]Cons[/b]: I don't know why this was tagged as an RPG on Steam, 'cause it sure isn't: you have no stats, no upgrades, no character interaction or dialog choice. You don't even really purchase and manage an inventory, gold serves as "points" that determine how much equipment you can bring in a mission, being able to swap out at full value any item in between chapters. It is a Hack & Slash in the most basic fashion, battles consisting merely of slashing in the wind, only knowing whether you hit anything if damage numbers appear, while the AI is monstrously bad (enemies just jiggle about, only occasionally chasing assuming you don't break line of sight, like passing behind a chair). Voice acting is horrible, the story is rather poor, character progression is absent, and having up-to-date resolution doesn't save the graphics that have aged so badly that most 3D Fantasy early access indie titles are doing better than this blocky 2-Gen-Old world. 

[b]Verdict[/b]: ★☆☆☆☆ - May it rot in your backlog

It's not horrible, but it is pretty bad by today's standards. I simply cannot get myself invested enough to ever play it again, leave alone complete a playthrough of even the first campaign. Maybe once upon a time it was considered a good game, but I can't see how I could recommend it to anyone, even for the low price.

Enclave is the sort of game where I wish Steam had a recommendation option that was somewhere between thumbs up and thumbs down. For a 3D game, the graphics surpisingly hold up well, but the combat is awkward and frantic. This is a problem because combat is everything in this game.

More like the Heretic series than a full-fledged RPG, Enclave's design in 2019 isn't that interesting: No character customization akin to attributes or skill points. A lack of enemy diversity. Instead, you progress along arcade-like beat-em-up stages where you collect gold in order to buy equipment for classes that you unlock as you reach certain points in the story. The classes do play differently enough, but the core gameplay isn't so different: frantically click the mouse until the enemy is dead, back-stepping in order to avoid getting hit.

When you complete the game, you unlock the Dark Campaign, where you can re-play the game from the perspective of the villains. After reading that the Dark classes are basically the same as the Light classes, I didn't have much interest in it. The Light Campaign took 5 hours to complete, so I imagine the Dark Campaign would amount to the same.

Nevertheless, Enclave does present a decent challenge even on the medium difficulty, sometimes on account of the combat's awkwardness but often times for legitimate reasons. Ultimately, I lean toward recommending the game in support of the recent trend where studios revive their old products for Steam. And I can't ignore that despite the game's flaws I still felt compelled to finish the campaign.

Enclave is an old (from 2002) third-person fantasy action game with hack-and-slash combat. I have no idea why it’s often called an ARPG on Steam. There are no dialogs or decisions to make, and you can’t gain experience points or improve attributes. Since there are also no quests, combat is the main focus here.

The story is fairly typical for a fantasy game. The world has been split in two by a war between the forces of light and darkness. You can choose between two campaigns at the beginning, either the Light or the Dark path. Both have about 15 levels if I remember correctly. Each gives you a different perspective of the story and also has completely different playable characters, each with their own abilities. Some characters are only unlocked after completing a certain level or if you found all the gold within it.

The objective in each level is to kill all the enemies and collect as much hidden gold as possible. The levels are well-designed and often have multiple paths you can take and some hidden secrets. Gold can also be exchanged for better equipment and potions before starting the next one.

Fighting is generally very fast and fluid but kept simple, and thanks to the different character classes like knights, mages, and assassins, it's also quite versatile and satisfying. There are lots of different enemies and also some difficult boss fights. The levels also get progressively more difficult. The game does a good job of balancing exploration and combat. Occasionally there are problems with the hitbox and you can't hit your target.

The graphics still look decent. It’s dark and gritty, with places like bleak castles and creepy forests. The soundtrack is also really good and creates a great dark fantasy atmosphere.

There is unfortunately no decent save system. You get checkpoints sometimes, but they don't come very often. Die at the wrong time and you'll probably have to restart the entire level.

The game might be a bit older, but I still really enjoyed it. If you see it on sale, I think it’s worth picking up.

This game is five bucks but is easily worth $30 or more, despite being 16 years old. It's a high quality hack-n-slash, RPG-lite fantasy adventure game in which you can play as a number of different character classes, through a bunch of really well built levels that are atmospheric and detailed with very good art design. The gameplay is smooth, responsive, and satisfying. Each character plays differently, adding a great amount of variety to the game. The story is swell, and to make things even better, there are two campaigns, not only one. In the light campaign you play as the good guys, fighting evil and laying waste to their plans; in the dark campaign you play as the bad guys, often times playing levels that you've seen before, but from a different vantage point, overlapping with the events that occurred in the light campaign. Both campaigns can be played through, and all their secrets found, in under 20 hours. 

This is a game that feels big and epic, but with a straight forward design that makes it a breeze to play through and fully explore in a couple weeks. However, the replay value is high, warranting more attention than one playthrough can give. This is a really well done game that I never heard about when it was released. 

The graphics, the music, the gameplay, and the combination of character styles and level design/aesthetic all come together to make a tight, superbly crafted action adventure fantasy game with semi-RPG elements that is endlessly fun, and always worth revisiting.

I'll try to be as fair as possible with this game. I've played both campaigns on difficult setting with 100% gold, though I had sometimes the urge to just quit the game. First of all, the game looks neat, especially by 2002 standards, the basics of gameplay are pretty easy to learn, the AI is ok and the soundtrack is really atmospheric. So much for the positive aspects of the game.
The story is rather lame, run-of-the-mill fantasy with some steampunk elements. But the cutscenes and the presentation of the story make up a little for the weak story. 
The biggest problem with the game are the messed up hitboxes. And that's a big issue in a hack 'n slash game. Arrows going right through enemies, melee fighters can't hit enemies on stairways if they are below them and missiles going right through massive obstacles. That seems to be intended for magic missiles, but I have noticed some examples where enemy bowmen attacked me through a solid wall while I couldn't hit them, which is pretty frustrating. Also, the 1st person view is rather glitchy, especially in narrow spaces.
The balancing is a mess. Sorcerers spam homing missiles at you which drain 1/4 of your life AND do damage over time while most melee fighters are push overs. Since the overall difficulty isn't very high (except for level 13 in the light campaign, that one was really tough), you can rush through most of the levels. You can beat this game with difficult setting and a 100% score in less than 15 hours.
I've never even read a single word about bugs referring to this game, but it has its fair share of them. Enemies dropping of cliffs who were supposed to drop gold => 100% no achievable. Traps not triggering. Even important NPCs tend to get stuck in the environment, so you have to start all over again. To be fair, most of the levels are pretty short (sometimes even ridiculously tiny), so that's not a big problem. 
In summary this game could have used a lot of testing, it feels a little unfinished in some places. But for 5 € you can't go wrong, and as a hack n slash fan you should definitely try this one out.

back to the game, enclave  certainly is somewhat dated, old school fantasy action game with ver limited rpg elements. the graphics were a joy to behold back in the day and still they hold up pretty well. the gameplay though is not that impressive. hit detection as mentioned by many is just utter crap. especially with melee weapons whole thing becomes a big clunky mashing game. there is a parry mechanic but i was never able got around to it. and this hit detection thing makes game really difficult. so what we have is not a challenging game because of it's design but rather because of the bad mechanics which is the worst kind of challenge. my advice is to use ranged characters in medium and hard difficulties and melee character in easy difficulty.

A bit of a rough little game.

There are 2 campaigns a Light and a Dark one.
You have to play through the Light one first to get a "code" to unlock the Dark one.
I recommend doing it in that order because the Dark campaign is harder at the start so get used to how things work in the Light one first.

There are different classes that get unlocked as you progress through the campaign.
You get access to better weapons, armour and such as you progress.

The stuff to collect like gems/gold are at times hidden so look around the level you go through. The more gold you get the better upgrades you can afford.

Using anything ranged can be a true hassle unless you go for the "shotgun" way with a bow which still can be a hassle with some enemies never being still enough and keeps shooting while moving around.

I recommend using medium difficulty for the first time as you get checkpoints then. They do cost 10 gold to use if you die. If you play on hard you play without checkpoints and it can be annoying since there are enemies that can 1-shot you or you fall to your death trying to get that gem/gold in a hard to get spot.

Enjoyed the game with the fixes below to get the game to run well. Never had any crashes whatsoever.

To get the game to run well I had to set the mouse polling rate to 125Hz. Without this turning the character made things go really weird and enemy behaviour was really odd. Found out about this on PCGamingWiki.
I also used the d3d8tod9. If you google it, it should be on Github.
To get the game to run in 1920x1080 I just edited the config file environment.cfg and set VID_MODE=1920 1080 32 60

Enclave is a medieval fantasy action game with a focus on using the gold you collect during levels to customize your character(s) before heading into the next area. The gameplay, at it's core, is satisfying and precise, and the game was an early adapter of the dynamic hitbox system that we see being used in newer action games. Unfortunately, that is where my praise for the game ends and my indifference towards it begins. Enclave is a good game.

Now, take my word for what it's worth because I am very, very much biased in favor of this game; I've completed it at least ten times on disc with another two since I purchased it on steam.
But, in my opinion, the fact I like it enough to have played it this many times is something of a statement as to it's quality.

The pros are easy to list:
-Very intuitive.
-Fast paced.
-Hitboxes are very much what you'd expect.
-Hitting someone with a melee weapon has the weight and impact you'd expect.
-The way the missions are handled makes shooting for the 100% both very much doable and rewarding.
-The paradox of "But I might need it later" never arises. You use what you need, when you need it, and it's bloody satisfying blasting a bunch of armored knights with a bomb.
-No serious difficulty spikes; the game picks up the pace as you go along, not suddenly bombards you with something unreasonable you've never seen before.
-Stealth works the way you'd expect.
-Multiple weapon types that actually feel different and require different timings for their attacks to actually land. Each of the several staves also has a very different main and secondary attack.
-Has a great cast of diverse characters for you to play as that actually have an impact on their playstyle; each of them has different equipment that they can use, different size hitboxes, different health and damage modifiers.
-Locational damage is very accurate and makes aiming for the most vulnerable part of your enemy a good way of removing them. This mechanic works well with the fact different characters have different armor types for different sections of their body, depending on armor class.

The cons are also easy to list:
-It's too short.
-Sound design. On multiple occasions I found the voice lines got sped up, raised in pitch or what-have-you.
-It's duration leaves something to be desired.
-Soundtrack is not that great.
-It's very, very brief.
-It's pretty old, and hasn't aged too well in most areas.
-It's gone too quickly.
-The story is stupid. Not even funny stupid, just flat out stupid. It's not offensive or anything, though.
-And yeah, it's length is insufficient.
-By now I'm so proficient in this game I can complete any mission of either campaign with just the starting bow and arrows, armorless and without consuming health potions. Send help.
-It's clock-time isn't all too great.

I've tried to like this game, loading it up a few times to get through several missions, but I end up giving up due to frustration with the controls. It is not an RPG, it is a hack and slack action game, and it's unfortunate when the worst part about an action game is the action.

Simply put, I find the controls too clunky and the collision detection spotty at best. The melee animations aren't just for style, the way your character swings a weapon is paramount to efficient combat, and I found getting the character to swing the way I want them to in a given situation to be inconsistent. Frequently my character would be wildly swinging a weapon over the head of my enemy while he freely hewed me in the chest. And I know that numerous times my weapon animation would pass right through an enemy to no effect, even if I knew I was within range.

It doesn't help that many of your enemies in the game are significantly shorter than most of your playable characters and it is a struggle to find the exact camera angle required to swing down at them without essentially staring at the floor. On top of that, just navigating certain narrow spaces became a chore as I found it unpredictable at to when I would bump up again a wall, box, rubble, etc and when I would slide past.

It's not that the entire game is totally awful. Obviously the graphics are dated given the game's age, but the art style still holds up nicely. The music fits the setting and tone very well, provided a great backdrop for the action. And for the story, while it didn't seem like anything super unique, I was genuinely interested to see what would happen next. But when it comes to recommendations, even if the game was inexpensive I just feel there are so many other games, even older, classic games such as this, that would be better worth one's time.

Enclave is a really fun hack and slash. It's simple but enjoyable gameplay sees you travel through 13 different missions which are basically "kill everyone and get to the end" with sometimes a fairly simple secondary task thrown in.

Unfortunately, the game's hit detection is a really off, especially when playing melee characters. Hits that should hit don't and if you're on the higher point of a slope to your enemy you'll just swing over their heads while they hack at your knees. There are a few levels, particularly in the Dark campaign, where this becomes a real problem.

There are also a few other weird instances like enemies being stuck in scenery and the game "compensating" by throwing them across the room. One level with spiral staircases causes all kinds of craziness. And enemies will often jump off cliffs to their deaths, which is admittedly funny.

Still, it's not enough to totally ruin the experience and if you can get it cheap it's well worth the 12-14 hours to play through.

This is a fantastic (yet flawed) fantasy action game that I feel is very underappreciated.

Enclave is often pretty janky and is filled with frustrating moments but even despite that I periodically find myself revisiting it. There's a lot of charm to it and while the story isn't anything to write home about, the gameplay is fun (most of the time) and the music is fantastic.

The game is split between good and evil campaigns and they could have easily just reused maps for each level, but while there is some overlap, there's a lot that's unique to each campaign. There are plenty of character classes that are better suited for different play styles and while I do feel some levels are better for specific characters, I feel like you can swap out characters pretty effectively in most cases. The game also includes bonus levels with their own gimmicks, which isn't necessary but a welcome addition.

The level up system is entirely currency based, which encourages level exploration and encourages you to replay missions to find any loot you may have missed.

Ultimately while it does have a lot of strengths, the flaws are mostly in the glitches you'll find along the way, some very cheap deaths, one shot kills, or the sometimes awful hit detection. These aren't problems you'll constantly deal with, but they happen enough to make note of.

With all that being said, despite its flaws, this is a great game with great music, art direction and one that's worth playing if you're into fantasy games.

Enclave is an absolute gem of its time. Made by the people of Starbreeze Studios, same ones who brought us the emotional [b]Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons[/b], the horror of [b]The Darkness[/b] and the fun times of [b]Payday2[/b]. Even back then, in the early 2000's they were people with sensible taste and a knack for developing simple ideas into fully fledged masterpieces. They seized the opportunity to make a game for the (back then) brand new Xbox and wanted to showcase the consoles potential. So they made this beautiful game.

When it comes to gameplay Enclave offers a third-person 3D hack-and-slash action adventure experience. Many (even Steam) consider it an RPG, but it truly is not. Just because you can choose whether to have your character upgraded or stock, doesn't really mean that you are "[i]playing a role[/i]". There is no real choice in the matter. The progression is there, but i can hardly consider it offering you a role to fit in. 
But what this game lacks in buzzword features makes up in enjoyable moment-to-moment combat encounters and varied enemies and environments to interact with. I cannot stress this enough but... [b]FOR ITS TIME[/b] 25 levels and 12 playable characters was more then enough to keep you entertained for a long time. Even now you can spend up to 10 hours trying to find the best-fitted fighter for any particular mission at hand.

The maps are vast and highly reword exploration with either in-game currency, a hidden access path to skip an encounter, or even a bonus map. Even more, a curious player is reworded for their thoroughness the moment when they collect all the gold pieces scattered throughout all the levels of the chosen campaign. On the Light Campaign you get the [i][b]9320 Battle Droid[/b][/i], and on the Dark Campaign you get [i][b]Fetica[/b][/i]. These are just overpowered characters to help you destroy your enemies in a much more enjoyable way.

Coming to the story element of the game, it is just a classic good versus evil story, but lived from both perspectives. Sadly, none of them are nuanced in any way. The good guys are good for the simple reason that they oppose the bad guys and vice-versa. They don't even try to show the bad guys from an other perspective when you play as them. If you actually pay attention and listen to the cutscenes, you'll get an actual reason for all of the events unfolding in the game. But the inciting event that triggers everything is just a classic "[i]evil demon wants to conquer the world for the sake of being evil[/i]". And don't get me wrong, it was/is/will forever be enough for me, but don't come to this game hoping for any sort of character development.

In conclusion this game blessed my very early years of gaming with its simplistic core mechanics and with its potential for replayability. The artstyle is charming for its clarity in designs and the theme and tone of the game match very well with its core idea. I would never be where i am without this here piece of software.

One of those numerous B class games which did not give you any unrealizable promises, but in fact was fun enough to spend hours after school. Back in the days I played Enclave from my friend's disc. Good memories. Later I got new PC, while he somehow managed to break his disc. Thus, I lost an access to the game for a rather long time... And it was great to find the game on Steam years later. 

There was no any innovative gameplay mechanics or mindblowing story. I'd say that most aspects here were typical for such kind of games. But still, it had a lot of classes to try, gear to choose, and secrets to find. It had some replay value. You could play both as good and evil. Different classes could change your gaming experience drastically.

I decided to give it a try not so long ago and for it's age, I must say, it looks surprisingly good. I finished one campaign, found all the secrets, and it was interesting enough. The game is rather hard (by today's standards), there is no check poihnts, so keep it in mind. I did not encounter any bugs, but sometimes had rare crashes.

As to adware controversy... Well, yeah, ugly situation to say the least. I bought the game not so long ago and thus, was rather late to the "party". But from my side I can say that at this moment there is no adware and it doesn't redirect you anywhere. Thus, the problem was fixed and it is safe to get the game.

I've enjoyed my time with Enclave and so could you, but only if you're willing to turn many blind eyes to its defects.
